This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) shares fell 1.82% to $58.29 as of 11:05 a.m. ET in regular trading on November 10, giving back part of Monday's 5.49% jump. Chip shares cooled after October consumer prices came in hotter than expected, lifting December rate-hike odds to about 84%.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Signs with INTC.

Is INTC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

INTC GF Value chart

Intel's own guidance sets the tone. Third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion, with data center and AI sales up 78% to $7.3 billion and foundry up 58%. Client computing slipped 5% to $8.1 billion. Fourth-quarter guidance calls for revenue of $15.0 billion-$16.0 billion and a GAAP gross margin of 37.1%, down from 43.0%. Trefis noted that management expects industry PC units to fall about 12% in 2026 and 10% in 2027.

The guidance midpoint implies a 6.1% sequential revenue decline alongside a 5.9-point gross margin squeeze, so data center growth cannot yet offset the PC drag. GuruFocus scores Intel at 70/100, with Momentum 9/10 and Profitability 7/10, but GF Value Rank just 1/10. At $58.29, the shares trade 69.15% above the $34.46 GF Value, which GuruFocus calls "Significantly Overvalued." Momentum is carrying the valuation. The January fourth-quarter report, and whether gross margin holds near 37%, is the next test.

Thursday, November 5 represented the worst trading session for the U.S. market in over a year. the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52%, the S&P 500 fell 4.36%, and the Dow shed 3.44%, as Wall Street's post-midterm optimism could not last long. Concerns around a potential weakness in AI spending reversed the post-election rally and led to almost $2.5 trillion wiped out of the U.S. market.

In the middle of this chaos, many names showed resistance and are still trading at their all-time highs. In our recent list of 10 Best All-Time High Stocks to Buy According to Wall Street, we uncover some of the stocks that still offer captivating upside to investors.

Various market sectors took a hit, including semiconductors which got affected the most. Technology was also amongst the worst-performing segments, dipping almost 8%. Just two days prior to the November 5 crash, we covered Warren Buffett's list of the 10 best stocks with attractive upside potential.

Situations like this trigger fear within the market. But for corporate insiders, including company executives and directors, it offers attractive entry points. These insiders have a more detailed understanding of their businesses compared to investors and analysts. They know about a company's growth prospects, margin potential, and product pipelines way before the market does.

Hence, a drop in share price does not necessarily mean that their stance on the company's outlook would also change. Through open-market purchases out of their own pockets, the insiders send some clear signals to the market. Unlike stock awards or option exercises, these purchases come out of personal savings, and no one is forced to make them.

title: Intel Is Still Up 61% in 2026 After Its October Crash: “A Broken Company,” or a Buy?
detail:
Intel Is Still Up 61% in 2026 After Its October Crash: “A Broken Company,” or a Buy?
Roxanna Maglangit
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 9:44 AM MST 5 min read
INTC
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Intel Is Still Up 61% in 2026 After Its October Crash: "A Broken Company," or a Buy? ©Daniel CHETRONI from Daniel Chetroni and DragonImages via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel stock is up 61% in 2026, but it's down 58% from its June 30 high after a weak fourth-quarter outlook on Oct. 29.

Intel isn't broken: data center and AI revenue rose 78% last quarter, and the company can't make enough server chips to meet demand.

That supply gap is helping AMD win server orders, and analysts have cut Intel's 2027 earnings estimate.

At 40x forward earnings the stock is still priced for a recovery, so the late-January report needs to show supply and margins coming back.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) stock is up 61% in 2026. That's what's left of a run that nearly quadrupled the stock by its June 30 high. It's now down 58% from that peak, and 43% in the past month, after a weak fourth-quarter outlook on Oct. 29.

Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) is there to take the server orders Intel can't fill.

Jim Cramer didn't hold back on Mad Money the next night: "it's a broken company because the company guided for a very weak 2027."

I think "broken" goes too far. But I'm not ready to buy yet, either.

A real recovery, paid for with new shares

Intel had a big year before the guide. Second-quarter revenue rose 25% to $16.1 billion, data center and AI revenue jumped 59%, and non-GAAP gross margin climbed to 41.8% from 29.7% a year earlier. The third quarter beat Intel's own guidance, with revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, data center and AI revenue up 78% to $7.3 billion, and non-GAAP gross margin at 44.1%.

Intel is paying for more capacity partly with new shares. In August, it sold stock at $95 a share and upsized the offering to $20 billion from $15 billion. Its third-quarter release puts the final total at $23 billion.

TIKR tracks 49 analysts on Intel. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Intel, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Intel's Analyst Ratings

Then the guide came up short

Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion, against the roughly $17.1 billion analysts expected. It also guided non-GAAP gross margin down to 38% and non-GAAP EPS to $0.25. CFO David Zinsner said Intel sees "the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year."

Supply hurt too. An Oct. 14 explosion shut Intel's Kiryat Gat fab in Israel for about two weeks, at a cost of about $300 million of revenue. And short supplies of substrates are capping its Xeon server chip shipments. Management also called 2027 an "investment year."

title: CEO Lip-Bu Tan’s 150,000-Share Purchase Wasn’t Enough to Stop the Slide in Intel Stock
detail:
CEO Lip-Bu Tan’s 150,000-Share Purchase Wasn’t Enough to Stop the Slide in Intel Stock
Pathikrit Bose
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 8:00 AM MST 6 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
An Intel sign out front of a corporate office by wolterke via Adobe Stock

Intel (INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan might have theorized that the sharp downturn in Intel stock had made its shares a value pick, and that his recent move to buy 150,000 shares of INTC stock could rescue it from a further downfall. However, shares fell even further after his Nov. 2 purchase, dropping as much as 10% on Nov. 5 alone before staging a recovery in the following days.

Intel stock now trades at around $59 per share, down roughly 8% from the average price of $64.73 at which Tan purchased his new shares. Notably, the CEO parted with about $9.71 million for the transaction. While a wider market selloff targeting the artificial intelligence (AI) trade could be seen as a reason for the recent downturn, that is not the whole picture. Let's take a closer look.

About Intel Stock

Founded in 1968, Intel is an integrated semiconductor company that designs, manufactures, packages, and sells processors and other semiconductor products. Its business can broadly be understood through two major segments; Intel Products designs and sells processors and related semiconductor products to customers, while Intel Foundry manufactures and packages semiconductors — from chips designed by Intel itself to those designed by external customers.

Valued at a market capitalization of $299 billion, INTC stock is up 61% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. Having said that, the stock's upward momentum so far this year may now be dragging its heels.

www.barchart.com
How Intel Is Falling Short

Intel's 18A process of making chips was supposed to bring its foundry business to life with external customers. Intel claimed that the 18A methodology delivers up to 18% higher performance at the same power, 38% lower power at the same performance, and 30% greater chip density compared with Intel 3. However, that has not resulted in Intel meaningfully competing with market leader Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM).

At the end of 2025, Taiwan Semiconductor (TSMC) disclosed that it had "deployed 305 distinct process technologies, and manufactured 12,682 products for 534 customers," with 74% of wafer revenue coming from 7 nanometer-and-below technologies. Although Intel does not disclose comparable figures, the latest quarterly results for both firms bear testament to TSMC's scale.
